Abelisauridae.note: Short-faced predators with arms reduced almost to nothing: the top carnivores of the Cretaceous southern continents.

Acrocanthosaurus.note: A high-spined carcharodontosaur eleven metres long, the top predator of Early Cretaceous North America.

Alamosaurus.note: The titanosaur that walked north: a thirty-metre giant that re-entered North America from the south after sauropods had been absent there for thirty million years.

Allosauroidea.note: The big three-fingered predators of the Jurassic and mid-Cretaceous, from Allosaurus to the carcharodontosaurs.

Amargasaurus.note: A short-necked sauropod with two rows of tall spines down its neck, perhaps carrying a sail or a display of horn.

Ankylosauridae.note: The club-tailed armoured dinosaurs: low, wide and plated to the eyelids.

Ankylosaurus.note: The last and largest ankylosaur, eight metres of fused armour ending in a tail club that could break a tyrannosaur's shin.

Anura.note: Frogs. The jumping body plan was in place by the Early Jurassic and has hardly changed.

Apatosaurus.note: The heavyweight of the Morrison plain -- a massively built diplodocid with a neck as deep as a horse's body.

Araneae.note: Spiders. Silk first for lining burrows; aerial webs came once there were flying insects worth catching.

Australovenator.note: A lightly built six-metre megaraptoran with huge hand claws: Australia's best-known predatory dinosaur.

Austroraptor.note: A five-metre, long-snouted Patagonian raptor with small arms -- South America ran its own line of dromaeosaurs.

Azhdarchidae.note: Giant toothless pterosaurs with stiff necks as long as a giraffe's, stalking prey on the ground like storks.

Baryonyx.note: A fish-eating theropod from the English Wealden with a crocodile snout and a thirty-centimetre thumb claw; fish scales were found in its stomach.

Beelzebufo.note: The 'devil frog': a 40 cm horned frog relative from Madagascar, big enough to take hatchling dinosaurs.

Blattodea.note: Cockroaches and their roachoid forerunners -- the commonest insects of the coal forests, and unhurried ever since.

Brachiosauridae.note: Sauropods built like giraffes, front legs longer than hind, holding the head twelve metres up.

Camarasaurus.note: The commonest sauropod of the Morrison Formation: a boxy skull, spoon-shaped teeth, and a build that browsed mid-height.

Camptosaurus.note: A mid-sized beaked plant-eater of the Morrison plain, walking on two legs or four.

Captorhinidae.note: Stocky lizard-shaped early reptiles, some with several rows of teeth for grinding plants -- among the first small herbivores on land.

Carcharodontosauridae.note: Shark-toothed giants that rivalled Tyrannosaurus in size, hunting sauropods across the mid-Cretaceous world.

Caseidae.note: Barrel-bodied synapsids with absurdly small heads: Cotylorhynchus reached four metres and was the first really large plant-eater on land.

Ceratopsidae.note: The great horned dinosaurs -- a North American radiation, each genus with its own arrangement of horns and frill.

Ceratosaurus.note: A horned, blade-toothed predator that shared the Morrison plain with the larger Allosaurus.

Coelophysoidea.note: Slender, hollow-boned early theropods two or three metres long: the first widespread predatory dinosaurs.

Coleoptera.note: Beetles. From the Permian on, the most species-rich order of animals there has ever been.

Cotylorhynchus.note: The largest land animal of its day: a caseid with a body like a barrel and a head that looks borrowed from something a tenth its size.

Crocodylia.note: True crocodiles, alligators and gharials. Their range is a thermometer: they reached the Arctic in the Eocene and are tropical now.

Cynodontia.note: The therapsids with a secondary palate, differentiated teeth and probably fur: the line that produces mammals in the Late Triassic.

Deinocheirus.note: Known for fifty years only from its 2.4 m arms; the rest turned out to be a hump-backed, duck-billed giant ornithomimosaur.

Deinonychus.note: The wolf-sized raptor whose discovery in 1964 overturned the image of dinosaurs as sluggish reptiles.

Deinosuchus.note: A ten-metre alligator relative from both shores of the Western Interior Seaway; bite marks show it ate dinosaurs.

Diamantinasaurus.note: A stocky titanosaur from the Winton Formation of Queensland, found beside the predator that may have fed on it.

Diplodocidae.note: The whip-tailed sauropods -- Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Supersaurus: twenty-five metres and more of neck and tail on a comparatively light body.

Diplodocus.note: Twenty-six metres long and most of it neck and tail; peg teeth at the front of the jaw raked leaves off branches it never chewed.

Diptera.note: True flies -- midges, mosquitoes, hoverflies -- with the hind wings reduced to balancing knobs.

Dromaeosauridae.note: The sickle-clawed, feathered 'raptors', close cousins of birds, from crow-sized to six metres.

Dryptosaurus.note: A tyrannosauroid of Appalachia, the eastern island of Cretaceous North America, with long arms its western cousins had lost.

Embolomeri.note: Long-bodied, eel-like reptiliomorphs of the coal-swamp pools -- fish-eating ambush predators close to the ancestry of amniotes.

Enantiornithes.note: The 'opposite birds': toothed, clawed-winged fliers that were the commonest birds of the Cretaceous and left no descendants.

Eoraptor.note: A metre-long, light-boned dinosaur from the dawn of the group, with teeth suited to both meat and plants.

Europasaurus.note: A dwarf sauropod six metres long, shrunk by life on the islands of the Jurassic European archipelago.

Eutriconodonta.note: Shearing-toothed Mesozoic mammals, the carnivores of their world -- including the one found with a dinosaur inside it.

Exaeretodon.note: A boar-sized traversodont cynodont, the commonest herbivore of Ischigualasto -- and found in India too, across an unbroken Gondwana.

Formicidae.note: Ants. Rare in Cretaceous amber, then from the Eocene on the dominant small predators and soil-movers of nearly every land habitat.

Gallimimus.note: The largest ostrich-mimic, six metres long, built to outrun Tarbosaurus across the Nemegt floodplain.

Gasparinisaura.note: A small Patagonian ornithopod known from many individuals, with gizzard stones still in its belly.

Gondwanatheria.note: Gnawing, high-toothed mammals unique to the southern continents; Madagascar's Adalatherium shows they could reach the size of a badger.

Hadrosauridae.note: Duck-billed dinosaurs, chewing with hundreds of stacked teeth and travelling in herds from Alaska to Antarctica.

Herrerasaurus.note: One of the earliest dinosaurs of all: a three- to six-metre predator from Ischigualasto, when dinosaurs were still a minor part of the fauna.

Heterodontosaurus.note: A turkey-sized early ornithischian from the Karoo with three kinds of teeth, including tusks, in one jaw.

Huayangosaurus.note: One of the earliest stegosaurs, from Middle Jurassic Sichuan, still with teeth at the front of its jaws.

Hymenoptera.note: Sawflies first, then wasps, bees and ants. Their rise tracks the flowering plants they came to pollinate.

Hypsilophodon.note: A two-metre sprinter from the Isle of Wight -- the small, fast plant-eater of the Wealden floodplain.

Iguanodontia.note: The big beaked plant-eaters with grinding tooth batteries, from Camptosaurus to the duck-bills -- the commonest large herbivores of the Cretaceous.

Isoptera.note: Termites: social cockroaches that digest wood with the microbes in their gut, and recycle most of a tropical forest's dead timber.

Kannemeyeriiformes.note: The big tusked dicynodonts of the Triassic -- ox-sized, beaked herbivores found on every part of Pangaea.

Kentrosaurus.note: Tendaguru's stegosaur: plates over the shoulders giving way to long paired spikes down the back and tail.

Koolasuchus.note: The last of the giant temnospondyls, five metres long, surviving in the cold rift-valley rivers of polar Australia where crocodiles could not live.

Kunbarrasaurus.note: Australia's most complete dinosaur: a sheep-sized armoured ankylosaur preserved with its last meal of ferns and fruit.

Leaellynasaura.note: A small, big-eyed ornithopod from Dinosaur Cove, which lay inside the Antarctic Circle: it lived through months of winter darkness.

Lepidoptera.note: Moths from the Jurassic, butterflies from the Cretaceous: scaled wings and, once flowers existed, a coiled tongue to reach nectar.

Lufengosaurus.note: The common early sauropodomorph of Yunnan, six to nine metres long; embryos in its eggs preserve some of the oldest known organic remains in a dinosaur.

Majungasaurus.note: The top predator of Late Cretaceous Madagascar -- a short-snouted abelisaur whose tooth marks on its own kind are clear evidence of cannibalism.

Massospondylidae.note: Mid-sized early sauropodomorphs of Early Jurassic Gondwana and beyond; nests of Massospondylus eggs show the young hatched toothless and helpless.

Megalosauridae.note: Robust Jurassic predators seven to ten metres long -- the family of the first dinosaur ever named.

Moschops.note: A thick-skulled, barrel-chested dinocephalian of the Karoo: a three-metre herbivore built for head-butting.

Muttaburrasaurus.note: An eight-metre Australian ornithopod with an inflated, hollow snout -- probably for calling across the polar forests.

Nigersaurus.note: A sauropod with a vacuum-cleaner mouth: five hundred teeth along the square front edge of a featherweight skull, cropping plants at ground level.

Nodosauridae.note: Armoured dinosaurs without tail clubs, relying on shoulder spikes; often found washed out to sea.

Notosuchia.note: Land-living crocodile relatives of the southern continents: long-legged runners, some with mammal-like teeth, some plant-eaters.

Odonatoptera.note: Dragonflies, damselflies and their giant Palaeozoic cousins the griffinflies: aerial predators for 325 million years.

Ornithomimosauria.note: Ostrich-mimic dinosaurs: toothless, long-legged, fast, and probably omnivores.

Orthoptera.note: Grasshoppers, crickets and katydids: the singing insects, and the great grazers of the insect world.

Oviraptorosauria.note: Beaked, crested, feathered theropods -- found brooding on their nests like birds, which is what their name's 'egg thief' got wrong.

Pachycephalosaurus.note: A bipedal plant-eater with a skull roof domed twenty-five centimetres thick, ringed with knobs and spikes.

Parasaurolophus.note: A duck-bill with a two-metre hollow crest swept back from its skull: a resonating tube for low-pitched calls.

Patagotitan.note: Thirty-seven metres and some sixty tonnes: among the largest land animals known, from a single Patagonian quarry of six individuals.

Plateosauridae.note: Long-necked, bipedal plant-eaters up to ten metres: the first dinosaurs to grow large, found in herds in Late Triassic Europe.

Procolophonidae.note: Squat, spiny-cheeked parareptiles a hand or two long. They crossed the end-Permian extinction and were everywhere in the Triassic.

Pteranodon.note: A crested, toothless fish-eater with a seven-metre span, soaring over the seaway that split North America.

Pterosauria.note: The flying reptiles: wings of skin stretched on one enormously long finger, from sparrow-sized to the span of a small aircraft.

Pulmonoscorpius.note: A 70 cm scorpion of the Scottish coal-age forests, with compound eyes and book lungs -- a land hunter, not a swimmer.

Rapetosaurus.note: Madagascar's titanosaur, known from one of the most complete sauropod skeletons of the Cretaceous.

Rauisuchia.note: Crocodile-line archosaurs that walked upright on pillar legs: the top land predators of the Triassic, before dinosaurs had the role.

Rhoetosaurus.note: Australia's Jurassic sauropod, about fifteen metres long -- one of very few windows on the continent's Jurassic land life.

Rhynchosauria.note: Pig-sized reptiles with a parrot beak and shearing tooth plates. In places they are half of all the fossils found -- then gone by the Norian.

Riojasaurus.note: A heavy ten-metre sauropodomorph of Late Triassic Argentina, already walking on all fours.

Saltasaurus.note: A small titanosaur studded with bony armour plates -- the discovery that showed sauropods could be armoured at all.

Sanajeh.note: A 3.5 m snake fossilised coiled around a titanosaur egg in a nest, waiting for the hatchling.

Sarcosuchus.note: 'SuperCroc': a twelve-metre, eight-tonne crocodile relative of the Cretaceous rivers of the Sahara and Brazil.

Saurosuchus.note: A seven-metre rauisuchian, the apex predator of Ischigualasto while the first dinosaurs ran about its feet.

Scorpiones.note: Scorpions: among the first arachnids ashore, and scarcely changed in outline since the Carboniferous.

Serpentes.note: Snakes: limbless lizards that swallow prey whole. They diversify after the Cretaceous, alongside the small mammals they eat.

Shantungosaurus.note: The largest ornithischian known: a flat-headed duck-bill fifteen metres long from Shandong.

Simosuchus.note: A pug-nosed, plant-eating crocodile relative from Madagascar, less than a metre long and armoured like an armadillo.

Sphenodontia.note: Lizard-like but not lizards. Worldwide in the Mesozoic; today one species, the tuatara, survives on New Zealand's offshore islands.

Spinosauridae.note: Crocodile-snouted, fish-eating theropods of river deltas and coasts.

Stegosauria.note: The plated dinosaurs: small heads, tall back plates and a spiked tail.

Steropodon.note: A Cretaceous monotreme known from an opalised jaw at Lightning Ridge -- platypus relatives are at least this old.

Suchomimus.note: An eleven-metre spinosaur of the Sahara's Cretaceous rivers, with a long, narrow, fish-trap snout.

Tapejara.note: A Brazilian pterosaur carrying a tall sail-like crest on a short, parrot-beaked skull.

Temnospondyli.note: Crocodile-shaped amphibians, from newt-sized to five metres, that ruled rivers and swamps for 200 million years before crocodiles took the job.

Tenontosaurus.note: A long-tailed ornithopod found again and again with the shed teeth of Deinonychus around it.

Testudines.note: Turtles: ribs turned into a box. On land, in rivers and at sea since the Late Triassic.

Therizinosaurus.note: A pot-bellied, ten-metre plant-eating theropod with the longest claws of any animal -- up to a metre each.

Therocephalia.note: Weasel- to wolf-sized therapsid predators. Unlike the gorgonopsians they got through the end-Permian extinction and hunted the Early Triassic.

Titanosauria.note: The last and largest sauropods, wide-hipped and often armoured. They are the big herbivores of every southern continent until the end of the Cretaceous.

Traversodontidae.note: Plant-eating cynodonts with broad grinding cheek teeth -- the commonest herbivores of many Gondwanan Triassic faunas.

Tyrannosauridae.note: The tyrant dinosaurs: huge heads, bone-crushing bites and two-fingered arms. Confined to western North America and Asia, the two halves of one land mass.

Tyrannosaurus.note: Twelve metres, eight tonnes, and the hardest bite of any land animal known. It lived only on Laramidia, the western island of a divided North America.

Utahraptor.note: The largest dromaeosaur: six metres long, with a slashing claw the length of a hand.

Yangchuanosaurus.note: The apex predator of Jurassic Sichuan, ten metres long, hunting Mamenchisaurus and the local stegosaurs.

Yutyrannus.note: A nine-metre early tyrannosauroid covered in long filament feathers -- the largest feathered animal known.
